tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Robert Brünauer in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: 7. Dynamik u. Vortrag, metodisch als Einheit u. Ausdruck der Synthese; wiederholt Gesd-Etude u. Brahms-Walzer No 2.

10. Trägt in mein Urlinieblatt des Jhrb. die Urlinie-studie ein,That is, the foreground graphs to the essays on Chopin’s etudes Op. 10, Nos. 5 and 6, published in the first volume of Das Meisterwerk in der Musik. ich korrigire Schichten u. dynamische Zeichen in dem Bild. Plötzlich meinte B.: er möchte die Préludes spielen „. . nur so, nur zu wissen wie man sie übt“Diary Oct 10, 1929: “Brünauer pays half, at the end of the lesson in which we have made such an interesting study for the first time [to discover] the methodical foundations of Chopin's dynamic markings; he says he would like to ask me: ‘Show me how one should practice the Preludes.’ I decline.” – Ich lehne streng ab u. rufe ihn zur Ordnung. Chopin: No 7, Cdur.

14. Etude Cdur No 7 neu; ich skizzire die Linie u. erkläre sie, lehre ihn, wie diese Etude geübt werden soll: zuerst die Finger 2 1, die Spannungen der Quint u. Sext, der Sinn der legato-Wirkung usw. wiederholt Stellen aus Schubert Me-
-nuett Hm.
21. Wiederholt u. arbeitet metodisch durch Nocturne Fisdur bis doppio movimento, jede Bewegung festgelegt.
24. Etude Fdur op. 10VIII neu, bis zum mittleren Teil.

28. Entrüstet sich über die offenbar in einer Gesellschaft gehörte Wendung von „Bruckner-Thränen“ in bezug auf die VIII. Sinf.A long entry in Schenker’s diary for October 28, 1929 begins: “Brünauer is very agitated and upset for being reproached for the tears wept on the occasion of hearing Bruckner's Eighth Symphony! Now since he is so constituted as to never reveal his emotions about similar things […] it merely remains for me to content myself with the suspicion that somewhere he was reproached for shedding tears as a sign of Bruckner's greatness, but that he was not in the position to rebut this foolish argument, so that in the end he suffered a setback. But since his excitement at the same time contained an appeal to my authority, which was supposed to decide about the worth or worthlessness of Bruckner, I could not now deny myself giving him a definition of Bruckner that would be useful to him and ease his burden […]” Bekennt sich zur Heimwehr! Nascht die Polonaise Cism Mittelteil.
31. Etude Fd bis zur Coda.
4. XI. Nascht aus Händels Suite Edur den Vortrag des Variationen Themas.
11. Das Bild der Etude Fd sehr sauber eingetragen, fast die Grenze des für ihn Erreichbaren. Spielt den 1. Teil nun fast ganz gut.

14. Aus Anlaß von Händel u. non legato über Liebhaber als meine Schüler, ich verfolge dieses Thema geschichtlich bis zu Brahms u. Bach, deren
Schüler ebenfalls Liebhaber waren.

18. Zeige Beispiele von Schönberg in einem seiner letzten Aufsätze zu Bachs 1. Cism-Präludium u. aus Mozarts Dissonanten-Quartett.Arnold Schoenberg, Zur Frage des modernen Kompositionsunterrichtes, Deutsche Tonkünstlerzeitung, (November 5, 1929); Eng. transl. Leo Black, On the Question of Modern Composition Teaching, in Style and Idea, ed. Leonard Stein (London: Faber & Faber, 1975), pp. 374–75.
25. Aus Anlaß der „Meistersinger“ über Wagner: eine Urlinie fehlt! Zeige Bilder der Eroica, Scherzo 1. Teil, Trauermarsch u. Rückleitung.

2. XII. Ueber Casals Konzert;The concert took place in the large hall of the Konzerthaus on Saturday November 30, with Pablo Casals, cello, and Otto Schulhof, piano. The program included Bach’s solo Suite in E and Beethoven’s Cello Sonata Op. 102, No. 2. Schuberts Menuett begonnen.
5. Chopin op. 25I begonnen; er liest den II. Bd. des Kontrapunkts, wie er sagt.
9. Ueber Beethovens Missa; Schubert Menuett wiederholt.
12. Bringt ein selbst verfaßtes Bild der Asdur Etude, auch ein Bild zur Coda der Fd Etude; ich trage Fingersatz ein.

16. Ueber das Philharmonische Konzert:Schenker heard the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra on December 14, 1929, and recorded a long entry in his diary for that day, which begins: “At 3 o'clock, on foot to the Philharmonic concert: Haydn, Symphony in G major, the so-called "Military", Respighi Roman Festivals, and Schumann's Symphony No. 1 in B major. Haydn was a failure!! Respighi enjoyed a great reception, in spite of not rising above the barbarisms of the Italian side-streets. [...]” Haydns sog. Militär-Sinfonie; Respighi usw.
19. Vortrag der Etude Asdur.

23. Vierhändig gespielt: Haydn Gdur-Sinfonie Adagio 6/8.Possibly the Symphony in G, Hob. I:81, the slow movement of which is an Andante (not Adagio) in 6/8. None of Haydn’s later G major symphonies has a slow movement in 6/8 meter.

30. Bringt eige-
-ne Walzer, ich improvisire Korrekturen.
2. I. Noch einmal die Walzer, ich vertage die Korrektur auf den 15.

9. Präludium von S. Bach aus dem Wohltemp. Klavier nach Linie, Metrik u. Dynamik aus Anlaß von v. Cubes Anfrage.In OJ 9/34, [20], January 2, 1930, Cube to Schenker: “For the Deutsche Tonkünstler-Zeitung I am working on an article Urlinie and Piano Teaching or A Lesson with Bach, and for this purpose I have chosen the first C major prelude from the Well-Tempered Clavier. I hope I have read it correctly.” – There follows an extended analysis of the Urlinie of the Prelude.
13.. Fehlt.
16. Holt zu einem politischen Gespräch aus über die Schwierigkeiten in Deutschland u. Oesterreich.
20. Ueber Romain Rolland aus Anlaß meiner Anfrage Anführung; Brahms Walzer Asd genau.
23. Das Bild der Coda aus der Etude Fd, gründlich noch einmal; Vortrag der Etude 25I, methodisch.

27. Ueber das Konzert Backhaus:According to the website of the piano manufacturers Bechstein (Bechstein/Backhaus), Wilhelm Backhaus performed the complete cycle of Beethoven’s 32 piano sonatas in Vienna and Paris in December 1929. ich zeige die Cism-Sonate, 1. u. 2. Satz, trage auch den Vortrag ein, arbeite ihn methodisch durch erkläre sogar die Urlinie.
30. Letzter Satz der Cism-Sonate flüchtig; das Bild von op. 25I neu gemacht, ich korrigire es.

3. II. Chopin Etude No 3, das Bild nachträglich verfaßt, ich
korrigire T. 1–16.
6. Fortsetzung der Etude No 3.
10. Zeigt ein Bild der Etude Sonate 27II, 1. Satz; ich korrigire flüchtig. Ueber den Begriff des Tonraumes.
20. Ed-Etude abgeschlossen; ich zeige aus Brahms Sinfonie Dd den 1. Ged.
24. Fragen zu den Diabelli-Variationen, Etude Fm neu.

27. „Ich möchte die Komposition nicht missen“! Ich rate ab u. zeige Schindlers Erstdruck („..könnte ich das Buch haben?“)Diary March 18: “During lunch, Dr. Brünauer appears and returns the first edition of Schindler” – presumably Anton Felix Schindler, Biographie von Ludwig van Beethoven (Münster: Aschendorff, 1840); at his death Schenker owned only a revised edition, which was published in 1909. Zeige Schumann zur Etude 25I.
3. III. Der Etude Ed Vortrag festgesetzt; Analyse des Brahms Walzer Asd.
6. Das Bild der Etude Fm; dann Anweisungen zum Ueben.

10. Ueber Sieburgs „Gott in Frankreich“.Friedrich Sieburg, Gott in Frankreich (Frankfurt: Societäts-Verlag, 1929), a book which became popular immediately and was translated into French (Dieu est-il français?) in 1930 and English (Who are These French?) in 1932. Reinhard Oppel referred to this book in his letter of April 17, 1930 (OJ 13/10, [102a]). — Diary March 10: “Brünauer has purchased Sieburg!! He stays ten minutes beyond his allotted time, even though Georg is already in the room, and asks if he can also play the Minuet by Schubert [...].” – Schenker had himself purchased the book five days earlier.
20. Die rein manuelle Darstellung der Etude Fm.
27. No 12 neu; ich erkläre die Linie.
31. Fehlt.

3. IV. Ueber Rameau u. Kürnberger, s. Jhrb. III.Rameau oder Beethoven: Erstarrung oder geistiges Leben in der Musik?, Meisterwerk III, (1930), 10–24 (Eng. transl., pp. 1–9). – Johann Philipp Kirnberger is not mentioned in the volume.
7. Das Bild des 1. Teiles der Cm Etude ganz.

10. Liest
seine Entgegnung an Rietzler vor.Diary April 10: “Brünauer surprises me with a splendid essay in opposition to Riezler in Die Musik. The difficulty of the musical content, as well as the language and form, are overcome with surprising ease; the essay has intellectual qualities, coming to a point in a satirical dialogue. In short, I could not have thought of anyone who could have managed this assignment so well on such a strictly objective basis!” – The article was Walter Riezler, Über die ‘Urlinie’, Die Musik, vii (April 1930), 502–10, cited in the Schenker Scrapbook (OC 2/p.80 item 5). Brünauer's essay was typed later that month and given the title: Die Urlinie: eine Entgegnung; a “carbon transcript” is preserved as OJ 21/24; Schenker received a copy on April 19 (diary). Weisse approved of Brünauer’s article and suggested sending it to Wilhelm Furtwängler with a view to its appearing in Die Musik (diary April 21). Furtwängler returned it rather than forwarding it to Die Musik (diary Sept 21, 1930), and the article remained unpublished. — For a complete transcription and English translation, see OJ 21/24, [1].
14. Mittelteil der Etude nach der Handschrift u. Vortrag.
17. Liest ein Einschiebsel zum Aufsatzi.e. Brünauer’s response to Walter Riezler; see lesson note for April 10, footnote. vor.
24. Noch einmal Gespräch über den Aufsatz.i.e. Brünauer’s response to Walter Riezler; see lesson note for April 10, footnote.

28. (von ¼4 – ½5h), ich lege aus Oppels Brief ein Beispiel von Quintfolgen aus Josquin de Pres vorIn his letter of April 17, 1930 (OJ 13/10, [102a]) received by Schenker on April 20, Oppel while praising Josquin des Pres remarks: “In the Gaudeamus [Mass] at “et incarnatus est” the following beautiful fifths (portamento), two-voiced, occur music example).”. u. das von Weisse gebrachte Rätsel aus op. 76IV von Brahms.Diary April 21, 1930: “Weisse asks a question about Brahms's Intermezzo in B major, Op. 76; he admits to being unable to find an Urlinie – perhaps ellipsis? Weisse would like to believe that ‘tonality’ and ‘diatony’ should be kept strictly distinct. Conceptually, the terms mean the same, they are synonyms; and this should not be overlooked when one relates ‘tonality’ in the narrower sense to the foreground, as the sum of all events, and ‘diatony’ to the background as the succession of tones in the octave. In other words, if the differences between foreground and background are emphasized too strongly, then the unity of the two concepts would be lost. — Diary April 28: “To Weisse (registered letter): I [...] show [him] the solution to Brahms's Op. 76, No. 4, in music and text, and ask at the end, ‘How would the conventional theory of form think about this?’”. — Diary April 30: “From Weisse (express letter): [...] for Brahms's Op. 76, No. 4 [...] he still proposes his own solution!”
1. V. (Statt 26. VI.Diary May 1: “Lessons given to Elias and Brünauer, to make up for June 26.”) Brahms 76IV, das Bild korrigirt.
8. Etude No 11, begonnen.
12. Bringt ein eigenes Bild, ich gebe Anweisungen zum Ueben.

15. Eroica 1. Satz (Toscanini)A Toscanini concert took place on May 19; program: Beethoven “Eroica” Symphony; Nocturne and Scherzo from Mendelssohn’s incidental music for A Midsummer Night’s Dream; Wagner, Venusberg music from Tannhäuser; Ravel, Bolero.
22. Er bringt das Bild zu Chopin Prélude No 9 Ed, ich korrigire flüchtig; Chopin No 11, das Bild der Coda zeige ich selbst.
26. Allerlei Fragen zu No 11.
29. (für die letzte Juni-Stunde) Etude Asd aus den Etudes Nouvelles; mündlich erledigt.

2-16. VI. Bilder der Asd Etude korrigirt.Diary June 2: “I work on Chopin's Etude, Op. 10, No. 10, for Brünauer, from 10:30 until 1 o'clock. — Brünauer wants to borrow and read Vrieslander's article "quickly"!” – The article in question was Otto Vrieslander, Heinrich Schenker, Der Kunstwart ix (June 1930, 43rd year), 181–89 (listed in Schenker’s scrapbook, OC 2/p. 80 item 3).

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Robert Brünauer in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: October 3: Etude in E minor, new; fingering.
October 7: Dynamics and performance, methodically as a unity and an expression of the synthesis; Etude in G major revisited, and Brahms’s Waltz No. 2.

October 10: He enters his Urlinie study into my Urlinie graph in the Yearbook; I correct the structural levels and dynamic markings in the graph. Suddenly Brünauer says that he would like to play the preludes “only in such a way as to know how one should practise them – I decline in the strictest terms and call him to order. Chopin: No. 7 in C major.

October 14:Etude No. 7 in C major, new; I sketch the voice-leading line and explain it, teaching him how this etude is to be practiced: to begin with, the fingering 2 1, the tensions in the intervals of a fifth and a sixth, the meaning of the legato effect, etc. He repeats passages from Schubert’s
Minuet in B minor.
October 21: He revisits and works methodically through the Nocturne in F major as far as the doppio movimento, every motion clearly determined.
October 24: Etude in F major, Op. 10, No. 8, new, as far as the middle section.

October 28: He is indignant about the expression “Bruckner tears,” evidently heard at a party, concerning the Eighth Symphony. Confesses to belonging to the Home Guard! Nibbles at the middle section of the Polonaise in C minor.
October 31: Etude in F major, up to the coda.
November 4: He nibbles at the performance of the variation theme from Handel’s Suite in E major.
November 11: The graph of the Etude in F major, entered very cleanly, nearly at the limit of what he is capable of. He now plays the first part very well almost throughout.

November 14: With reference to Handel and non legato, with concern for the amateurs who are my pupils, I follow this subject historically as far as Brahms and Bach, whose
pupils were likewise amateurs.
November 18: I show him examples from Schoenberg in one of his recent essays, on Bach’s first C minor Prelude and Mozart’s “Dissonance” Quartet.

November 25: With reference to Die Meistersinger, concerning Wagner: an Urlinie is absent! I show him graphs of the “Eroica”: the first part of the Scherzo, and the Funeral March and its retransition.
December 5: Chopin’s Op. 25, No. 1, begun; he is reading the second volume of my Counterpoint, so he says.
December 9: Concerning Beethoven’s Missa solemnis; Schubert’s Minuet revisited.
December 12:He brings a graph of the A major Etude that he made himself, also a graph of the coda of the F major Etude; I enter fingering.
December 16: Concerning the Philharmonic concert: Haydn’s so-called “Military” Symphony; Respighi, etc.
December 19: Performance of the Etude in A major.
December 23: The Adagio in 6/8 from Haydn’s Symphony in G major, played four-hands.

December 30: He brings
waltzes of his own composition; I improvise corrections.
January 2: Once again, the waltzes; I delay making corrections until the 15th.
January 9: J. S. Bach’s Prelude from the Well-Tempered Clavier, with respect to voice-leading line, metric organization, and dynamics, in connection with Cube’s question.
January 13: He is absent.
January 16: He launches into a political discussion about the difficulties in Germany and Austria.
January 20: On Romain Rolland in connection with my mentioning him; Brahms’s Waltz in A major played precisely.
January 23: The graph of the coda of the Etude in F major, once again thoroughly; performance of the Etude Op. 25, No. 1, methodical.
January 27: On Backhaus’s concert: I show him the C minor Sonata, first and second movement; I also enter the performance marks, working through them methodically, and even explain the Urlinie.
January 30: Last movement of the C minor Sonata, hastily. The graph of Op. 25, No. 1, remade; I correct it.

February 3: Chopin Etude No. 3, the graph made subsequently; I
correct bars 1–16.
February 6: Continuation of the Etude No. 3.
February 10: He shows me a graph of the Sonata Op. 27, No. 2, first movement; I correct it hastily. On the concept of tonal space.
February 20: E major Etude completed; I show him the first subject of Brahms’s Symphony in D major.
February 24: Questions about the Diabelli Variations; Etude in F minor, new.
February 27: “I don’t want to give up composing”! I advise him not to and show him the first edition of Schindler (“may I have the book?”). I show him Schumann on the Etude Op. 25, No. 1.
March 3: Performance for the Etude in E major determined; analysis of Brahms’s Waltz in A major.
March 10: On Sieburg’s Gott in Frankreich.
March 20:The purely manual representation of the Etude in F minor.
March 27: Etude No. 12, new; I clarify the voice-leading line.
March 31: He is absent.
April 3: Concerning Rameau and Kirnberger; see Yearbook 3.
April 7: The graph of the first part of the C minor Etude, complete.

April 10: He reads his
response to Riezler to me.
April 14: Middle section of the Etude according to the manuscript, and performance
April 17:He reads out an addendum to his essay.
April 24: Another conversation about his essay.
April 28: (from 3:15 to 4:30), I present an example of parallel fifths in Josquin de Pres, from Oppel’s letter, and the puzzle from Brahms’s Op. 76, No. 4 brought up by Weisse.
May 1: (in place of June 26). Brahms’s 76, No. 4; the graph corrected.
May 8: Etude No. 11 begun.
May 12: He brings his own graph; I give him instructions for practicing.
May 15: Eroica, first movement (Toscanini)
May 19: Second, third, and fourth movements.
May 22: He brings the graph of Chopin’s Prelude No. 9 in E major; I correct it hastily. Chopin No. 11; I show him the graph of the coda myself.
May 26: Various questions about No. 11.
May 29: (in place of the last lesson in June): Etude in A major from the Trois études nouvelles explained face-to-face.
June 2-16: Graphs of the A major Etude corrected.

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Angi Elias in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: 1. X. Allgemeines über Plan: Beethoven op. 10I.Diary Sept 25, 1929: “From Miss Elias and Miss Kahn (letters): confirmation.” See OJ 10/18, [4], September 23, 1929.

3. Händel Suite, Bild der Einleitung korrigirt.In OJ 10/18, [4], September 23, 1929, Elias states: “Now I hope to be able to dedicate myself once again to music, undisturbed as much as possible, and between now and October 1, as far as can be, to bring to a close the voice-leading sketch (Entwurf der Stimmführung) of the fugue by Handel begun in Vent.” – From the way Elias and Schenker refer to its various movements, the work by Handel was his Suite No. 2 in F major, HWV 427, on which she had already worked intensively between January and April 1929, and on which Albersheim, Brünauer, and Hoboken had also worked in 1928/29, all producing graphs. The movements are: 1. Adagio (“Einleitung”), 2. Allegro, 3. Adagio, 4. Allegro (Fugue).

5. Ueber Schindlers Erstdruck,Anton Felix Schindler, Biographie von Ludwig van Beethoven (Münster: Aschendorff, 1840) (at his death Schenker owned only the revised edition of 1909). erste Worte zum Gebrauch des Buches.
8. Diminution, Triller, Manieren zum 3. Händel-Stück.

10. Ueber das pro arte Quartett (Rundfunk):Radio broadcast October 9, 8 p.m., program: Mozart String Quartet in D minor; K. 421; Beethoven, String Quartet in B major, Op. 130; Debussy, String Quartet in G major, Op. 10. The Pro Arte Quartet was founded in Belgium in 1912; its members at this time were Alphonse Ornou, Laurent Halleux, Germain Prévost, and Robert Maas. Vortrag.

12. Schindler über op. 14I, II;Preserved in folder OJ 16/3 are five undated essays by Schenker, written in various hands: (1) “Schindlers Beschreibung von Beethovens Vortrag der Sonate Op. 14, No. 2 [und] Schenker’s Erläuterung hiezu“; (2) “Zitate aus Schindlers ‚Beethoven‘“; (3) “Auszug aus Schindlers ‚Beethoven‘“; (4) “Schindlers Beschreibung von Beethovens Vortrag …“; (5) “Beethovens Sonate Op. 14, No. 2, 1. Satz, T. 47–63,“ all unpublished. Published posthumously was: Heinrich Schenker, Ein Kommentar zu Schindler, Beethovens Spiel betreffen, Der Dreiklang 8/9 (Nov 1937/Feb 1938), 190–99, followed by Oswald Jonas, Nachtrag zu Schenkers Aufsatz über Schindler, ibid, 200–97. erkläre die Echtheit aus der Natur des Stoffes u. der Beobachtung; setze Riemanns AnalyseHugo Riemann, L. van Beethovens sämtliche Klavier-Solosonaten: ästhetische und formal-technische Analyse mit historischen Notizen, vol. 1 (Berlin: Max Hesse, 1918). in Vergleich.
15. Das Bild der Verzierungen korrigirt u. Fingersatz draufgesetzt.
17. Bild der Händel-Fuge begonnen.
19. Notirt was ich zu Schindler sage.See footnote 5, above.

22. Vortrag des 3. Händel-Stückes; ich zeige meine Korrektur an v. Hobokens op. 117I.Hoboken began work on Brahms's Intermezzo in E major, Op. 117, No. 1, on October 8, and handed Schenker a “corrected presentation (Darstellung)”. – A “philological-comparatist” (as apart from analytical) study by Hoboken of Opp. 117, Nos. 1–3, comparing the autograph with the Simrock and collected editions, is preserved at OC 14/2 (28-page typescript) and OC 14/3 (earlier typewritten amended draft), with a letter, OJ 89/3, [9] September 15, 1929 (= OC 14/1) accompanying his study, in which he remarks “I would have liked to investigate several matters more closely in a substantive way; I defer this now until such time as I will again visit you.”
26. Die Notizen zu Schindler durchgesehen u. ergänzt;See footnote 5, above. Beethoven Sonate Gdur, 1. Teil gespielt!

29. Hafner-Serenade unter Walter,Concert given on October 26 and 28, conducted by Bruno Walter, program: Mozart, Symphony in D major (“Haffner”), K. 385 (not the Serenade); Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde (soloists Rosette Anday and Julius Patzak). vierhändig Andante u. Menuett
gespielt.
31. Beginn der Korrektur des Bildes vom Mittelteil der Fuge.Diary Oct 30: “I work on the Handel fugue ([for] Elias).”
2. XI. Erläutere die Durchführung aus op. 14I zu Schindler.See footnote 5, above.

5. Ueber die Diabelli-Variationen von Schnabel gespielt.The recital by Artur Schnabel took place in the great hall of the Musikverein Building on November 4 at 12.30 p.m., program: Schubert, Sonata in C minor, D. 958; Mozart, Sonata in D major, K. 576; Beethoven, Diabelli Variations.
9. Ihre Schindler-Darstellung zu weit, ich dränge auf Kürzung.See footnote 5, above.

16. Spielt op. 14II, den 1. Satz ganz; über das Finale in Schuberts Cm-Sonate;See footnote 13, above. über den Plan: von Cm zu Esd als der III. Stufe, über A u. B.In the finale of D. 958, Schubert arrives at E minor in bar 169, via A minor in bar 145 and C minor (not B) in bar 157; E major is reached only at bar 213.

19. Ueber Schönbergs Beispiel in der Tonkünstler Ztg. Arnold Schoenberg, Zur Frage des modernen Kompositionsunterrichtes, Deutsche Tonkünstlerzeitung, (November 5, 1929); Eng. transl. Leo Black, On the Question of Modern Composition Teaching, Style and Idea, ed. Leonard Stein (London: Faber & Faber, 1975), pp. 374–75.
21. Korrektur der 1. Schicht in den Fugenbildern abgeschlossen.
23. Schindler-SchenkerSee footnote 5, above. fast ganz in Ordnung gebracht.

26. Zu Casals Konzert:The concert took place in the large hall of the Konzerthaus on Saturday, November 30, with Pablo Casals, cello, and Otto Schulhof, piano. The program included Beethoven’s Cello Sonata in D major, Op. 102, No. 2, and Bach’s Suite in E major for unaccompanied cello. aus op. 102II, 1. Satz, 2. Ged.
30. Erkläre das Andante aus op. 14II, sie spielt.

3. XII. zu Casals; berichtige den Vortrag des Durchgangs in op. 102II; über Casals sehr schönes non legato in Bachs Präludium Esd.The concert took place in the large hall of the Konzerthaus on Saturday November 30, with Pablo Casals, cello, and Otto Schulhof, piano. The program included Beethoven’s Cello Sonata in D major, Op. 102, No. 2, and Bach’s Suite in E major for unaccompanied cello.

5. Das Hin-
-tergrundgbild der Fuge verfaßt; ich zeige die Linie zu Brahms 117II.

7. Ueber SpaldingThe recital took place in the large hall of the Konzerthaus, Vienna, on December 6, 1929, with Albert Spalding, violin, and Andre Benoist, piano. u. Knappertsbusch;The fourth Tonkünstler subscription concert took place in the Musikverein Building on December 5 at 7.30 p.m., conductor Wilhelm Knappertsbusch, program: Schubert, Two Overtures in Italian Style; Clemens von Franckenstein, Dance Suite; Szymanowski, Violin Concerto (soloist Hugo Gottesmann); Brahms Symphony No. 2 in D major. die Durchführung aus op. 14II; sie zeigt ein neues Bild zur Berichtigung des im AufsatzA study of Anton Schindler’s notes on Beethoven’s piano playing, as interpreted by Schenker. See footnote 5, above. unterlaufenen Mißverständnisses.

10. Zum Rachmaninov-Konzert:Concert in the Vienna Konzerthaus on December 9 at 8 p.m.. Diary Dec 2: “To Miss Elias (express postcard): I shall gladly accept the tickets offered for Rachmaninoff.” die in der Mozart-Sonate Dd u. in der Ballade Gm, Sonate Bm, Walzer Esdur u. Asd begangenen Fehler; über Giesekings Vortrag des Beethoven Konzerts,Concert in the Vienna Konzerthaus on December 10 at 7:30 p.m, in which Walter Gieseking was the soloist in Beethoven’s Fifth Piano Concerto. 1. Satz.
14. Fortsetzung Gieseking: 2. u. 3. Satz des Beethoven-Konzertes; spielt den letzten Satz von op. 14II.
17. Sie spielt die Fuge nach meinen dynamischen Anweisungen.
21. Korrektur zu Schindler ganz abgeschlossen.See footnote 5, above.
24. Ueber Flaubert u. Stendahl.

1. V. Weisses Frage zu Brahms op. 76IV:Diary April 21, 1930: “Weisse asks a question about Brahms's Intermezzo in B major, Op. 76; he admits to being unable to find an Urlinie – perhaps ellipsis? Weisse would like to believe that ‘tonality’ and ‘diatony’ should be kept strictly distinct. Conceptually, the terms mean the same, they are synonyms; and this should not be overlooked when one relates ‘tonality’ in the narrower sense to the foreground, as the sum of all events, and ‘diatony’ to the background as the succession of tones in the octave. In other words, if the differences between foreground and background are emphasized too strongly, then the unity of the two concepts would be lost. — Diary April 28: “To Weisse (registered letter): I [...] show [him] the solution to Brahms's Op. 76, No. 4, in music and text, and ask at the end, ‘How would the conventional theory of form think about this?’”. — Diary April 30: “From Weisse (express letter): [...] for Brahms's Op. 76, No. 4 [...] he still proposes his own solution!” — An Urline-Tafel and a four-level graph of Op. 76, No. 4 in Elias’s hand survive at OC 34/45–48, cf. lesson note for May 22. das Bild korrigirt.

tei:div.tei:note: The lesson reports for Angi Elias in the original are written continuously, without paragraph breaks or separating punctuation. They have been separated here in the interests of legibility.
tei:div.tei:ab: October 1: General matters concerning plan: Beethoven Op. 10, No. 1.
October 3: Handel Suite, graph of the Introduction corrected.
October 5: Concerning Schindler’s first edition, my first words about the use of the book.
October 8: Diminution, trills and ornaments in the third movement of Handel.
October 10: Concerning the Pro Arte Quartet (on the radio): performance.
October 12: Schindler on Op. 14, No. 1 and No. 2; I profess its authenticity on the basis of the nature of the material and the observation; I place Riemann’s analysis next to it in comparison.
October 15: The illustration of the ornaments corrected, and fingering added to it.
October 17: Graph of Handel’s fugue begun.
October 19: She takes down what I say about Schindler.
October 22: Performance of the third movement of Handel; I show her my corrections to Hoboken’s Op. 117, No. 1.
October 26: Her notes on Schindler examined thoroughly and amplified; the first part of Beethoven’s Sonata in G major played!

October 29: Haffner Serenade under Walter; the Andante and Minuet
played four-hands.
October 31: Start of corrections to the graph of the middle section of the fugue.
November 2: I elucidate the development section from Op. 14, No. 1 in accordance with Schindler.
November 5: On the Diabelli Variations, played by Schnabel.
November 9:Her presentation of Schindler goes too far; I press her to shorten it.

November 16: She plays the first movement of Op. 14, No. 2, in its entirety. Concerning the finale of Schubert’s Sonata in C minor; concerning the plan to modulate from C minor to E major (as scale-step III) by way of A and B.
November 19: Concerning Schoenberg’s examples in the Tonkünstlerzeitung.
November 21: Correction of the first layer in the graphs of the fugue completed.
November 23: Schindler-Schenker almost completely put in order.
November 26: On Casals’s concert: from Op. 102, No. 2, the first movement, second theme.
November 30: I explain the Andante of Op. 14, No. 2; she plays.
December 3: On Casals: I correct his performance of the transition in Op. 102, No. 2; on Casals’s very beautiful non legato in Bach’s Prelude in E.

December 5: The graph
of the background of the fugue created; I show her the voice-leading line of Brahms’s Op. 117, No. 2.
December 7: On Spalding and Knappertsbusch; the development section of Op. 14, No. 2; she shows me a new graph, to correct the misunderstanding that arose in her essay.

December 10: On the concert given by Rachmaninoff: the mistakes made in Mozart’s Sonata in D major and in the Ballade in G minor, the Sonata in B minor and the Waltzes in E major and A major. On Gieseking’s performance of Beethoven’s Concerto, first movement.
December 14: Continuation of Gieseking: second and third movements of the Beethoven concerto. She plays the last movement of Op. 14, No. 2.
December 17: She plays the fugue in accordance with my dynamic markings.
December 21: Correction of the essay on Schindler fully completed.
December 24: On Flaubert and Stendahl.
December 28: Op. 22, new; she plays up to the development section, I make suggestions about the Urlinie.
January 2: The graph of Schubert’s Minuet in B minor; I explain the performance.

January 4: Brahms’s Serenade in D major played four-hands, first movement
and minuet.
January 7: She plays the entire Suite, for the last time.
January 9: The last movement of the Serenade played four-hands.
January 11: Op. 22: performance markings in the first movement entered.
January 16: J. S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier, Prelude No. 1, corrected.
January 18: Brahms’s Serenade: the last movement, with reference to the Urlinie and other things.
January 23: She repeats Beethoven’s Sonata in C minor (Backhaus concert); I add to the performance markings.
January 25: She copies out my performance markings and plays the first and second movements of Op. 27, No. 2.
January 30: Last movement: performance and Urlinie.
February 1: I elucidate the form of the Adagio of Brahms’s Serenade; she brings a portrait of Handel, on the occasion of her being my pupil for 25 years.
February 4: Revisit of Op. 27, No. 1 2 , and Brahms’ Serenade.
February 6: Revisit of Op. 27, No. 1 2 , and Brahms’ Serenade.

February 18: On Korngold’s critique of Furtwängler’s presentation of Brahms’s
Second Symphony. What a Furtwängler is capable, and not capable, of achieving: the first theme of the first movement!

February 20: On Korngold’s critique of Furtwängler’s presentation of Brahms’s
Second Symphony. What a Furtwängler is capable, and not capable, of achieving: the first theme of the first movement!
February 22: She presents me with the fair copy of the essay on Schindler. I correct the graph of the development section of Op. 22.
February 25: She revisits the Berceuse.
February 27: Once again, the graph of the development section of Op. 22.
March 1: She plays the Adagio from Op. 22, new.
March 4: Paganini Variations, book 2 taken up. She revisits the Chopin Waltz in A major: very good.
March 6: Schumann String Quartet in A major Op. 41, No. 1, four-hands after Kirchner, first and third movements (radio).
March 8: Schumann, second movement.
March 11: She brings the graph of Chopin’s Op. 10, No. 3.
March 15: Minuet of Op. 22, new.
March 18: Remarks on Furtwängler’s performance of Mozart’s E major and the Fifth Symphony.
March 20: Brahms Waltz in A major.
March 22: Op. 22 Rondo, new.
March 25: The graph of the first variation corrected.

March 27: I explain once more what Schindler says about
Op. 14, No. 1.
March 29: I show her Nagel and Marx on Op. 14, No. 2, and Op. 22; she plays the entire Rondo.
April 1: Fingering and technical matters for Variation 1.
April 3: She revisits Chopin’s Waltz in C minor, very good; then I show her the sources for Op. 117, Nos. 1–3.
April 5: Completion of Op. 22.
April 8: Variation 2, graph and fingering; I alert her to Riezler.
April 10: Work on the graph of Chopin’s Op. 10, No. 3.
April 12: Op. 26, new; theme, elucidation, performance.
April 15: The graph of the third variation corrected.
April 17: Work on the Etude Op. 10, No. 3.
April 19: With her nephew Peter and Mrs. Albrecht.
May 1: Weisse’s question about Brahms Op. 76, No. 4: the graph corrected.
May 3: Op. 26, variations 1 and 2, new.
May 6: Performance of Paganini variations 6–8.
May 10: Op. 26, variation 3.
May 13: Paganini graphs corrected as far as variation 11.
May 15-20: On Toscanini: concerning his performance of the Eroica.
May 22: Graph of Brahms op. 76, No. 4, very beautiful.
May 24: Op. 26 up to the last variation.

May 27: Paganini
as far as variation 12.
May 31: She revisits Brahms’s Serenade Op. 11 on account of the evening concert on the Josephplatz.
June 3: Paganini graphs continued and variations played.
June 5: Remaining things for the graphs of the Etude Op. 10, No. 3.
June 7: Op. 26: the first and second movements played.

tei:div.tei:ab: 8. X. Ueber das Jahrbuch oder eine Zeitschrift?The board of the Photogram Archive was at this time discussing the creation of a publication, provisionally known as Mitteilungen (“Communications”), through which to publish research conducted in the Archive, and debating its format. The plan came to nothing. — Schenker’s diary for October 8 contains a lengthy discussion of the funding of the planned Mitteilungen of the Archive. — The “Blatt” at the end of this entry may relate to a “philological-comparatist” (as apart from analytical) study by Hoboken of Op. 117, Nos. 1–3, comparing the autograph with the Simrock and collected editions, which is preserved at OC 14/2 (28-page typescript) and OC 14/3 (earlier typewritten amended draft), with a letter, OJ 89/3, [9], September 15, 1929 (= OC 14/1) accompanying his study, in which he remarks “I would have liked to investigate several matters more closely in a substantive way; I defer this now until such time as I will again visit you.” H. wünscht, daß die Hefte zwanglos erscheinen. Ich erkundige mich nach dem Einlauf. op. 117I: notiert meine Kritik auf sein Blatt.

11. Ueber die Ausführung eines Doppelschlags – das Pro Arte Quartett ist im Unrecht. Chopin Gism-, Am-, Em-Etude wiederholt. Kritik der RevisionsstudieRevisionsstudie: probably a textual commentary on Brahms’s Three Intermezzi, Op. 117, mentioned throughout Hoboken’s lessonbook notes for 1929/30, perhaps identifiable with the unpublished OC 14/2 (28-page typescript). fortgesetzt, No 1 abgeschlossen. Trage ihm auf, meine Korrekturen neu durchzuarbeiten.

15. Etude Esm: Erklärung der dynamischen Zeichen aus ihrem Grunde; Technik
Vortrag, Fingersatz. Uebergibt mir die korrigirte Darstellung von op. 117I

18. Etude Esm gespielt. Gehe meine Korrektur mit ihm durch.Diary Oct 17: “I work on the corrections for Hoboken.” Bach-Schemelli-Roth No 1,Herman Roth, ed., 25 Geistliche Lieder (aus dem Schemellischen Gesangbuch) für eine Singstimme und basso continuo (Leipzig: C. F. Peters, [n.d.]), a copy of which, with annotations in Schenker's hand, is preserved at OJ 25/1: No. 1 Auf, auf! die rechte Zeit ist hier, BWV 440. neu.

22. Zeige Oppels Kantate u. einige Fehler darin. Erbitte eventuell die Handschrift aus dem Archiv. Auf Weisse zurückkommend, zeige ich einen nach Galtur gerichteten Brief von WeisseProbably OJ 15/16, [62], August 5, 1929, beginning “Above all else, I feel the need to tell you of the joy that filled me during the past days by thinking through your concept of ‘tonal space.’ [...], and continuing: ‘My idea is to place you at the center of contemporary music theory, to show how you have brought to life one concept after another, […] I believe that today I have fully understand this matter, and I look forward to this project, which I have set myself!’” in dem nichts weniger als ein Abfall von mir sich durchaus kein Abfall von mir kundgibt. Roth No. 2,Herman Roth, ed., 25 Geistliche Lieder (aus dem Schemellischen Gesangbuch) für eine Singstimme und basso continuo (Leipzig: C. F. Peters, [n.d.]), a copy of which, with annotations in Schenker's hand, is preserved at OJ 25/1: No. 2 Ich steh’ an deiner Krippen hier, BWV 469. — Diary Oct 21: “I work on Bach–Schemelli for Hoboken.” neu. Bringt „Musikalisches Mancherlei“, darin eine Sonate von Ph. E. Bach.Diary Oct 22: “Hoboken brings the first edition of [C. P. E.] Bach's Keyboard Sonata in E minor and invites himself for 4:15 to the loudspeaker.” Ladet sich für Freitag ¼5h (!) zum Lautsprecher ein (Pessel),According to the radio listings in the Neue freie Presse, Jella Pessl performed a “sonata by Bach” on the harpsichord, in a program broadcast at 4:15 p.m. wir bitten ihn zum Tee.

25. Um 4h; dann nehme ich Stellung zu Fasch’s Sonate u. Em. Bach Gm, gespielt von Frl. Pessel, in bezug auf Linie u. Vortrag.Diary Oct 25: “A few minutes after 4 o'clock, Hoboken appears! [Jella] Pessl and [Frieda] Krause at work – already at 5 o'clock he stepped into the music room; he has brought nothing and stays until 6:45! I am obliged to anticipate the subject, which was actually his homework, and go through Fasch and C. P. E. Bach regarding line and performance; I go to Roth, No. 3, and so forth.” Roth No 3,Herman Roth, ed., 25 Geistliche Lieder (aus dem Schemellischen Gesangbuch) für eine Singstimme und basso continuo (Leipzig: C. F. Peters, [n.d.]), a copy of which, with annotations in Schenker's hand, is preserved at OJ 25/1: No. 3 Selig, wer an Jesum denkt, BWV 498. Linie usw., dazu Br. u. H.-Ausgabe. Desd
Etude die Hände einzeln durchgearbeitet; bleibt bis ¾7h!

29. Ueber Furtwänglers Darstellung von Bruckner u. Händel;The first subscription concert of the season took place in the great hall of the Musikverein Building on October 27, 1929 at 1 p.m., the Vienna Philharmonic conducted by Wilhelm Furtwängler, program: Handel, Concerto Grosso in D major, Op. 6, No. 5 (HWV 323), and Bruckner, Symphony No. 8 in C minor. über Walters Aufführung der Haffner-Sinfonie:Concert given on October 26 and 28, conducted by Bruno Walter, program: Mozart, Symphony in D major (“Haffner”), K. 385; Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde (soloists Rosette Anday and Julis Patzak). 4händig das Andante u. Menuett daraus gespielt. Etude Gesd. Fingersatz u. Vortrag; Roth No 4.Herman Roth, ed., 25 Geistliche Lieder (aus dem Schemellischen Gesangbuch) für eine Singstimme und basso continuo (Leipzig: C. F. Peters, [n.d.]), a copy of which, with annotations in Schenker's hand, is preserved at OJ 25/1: No. 4 Mein Jesu! was für Seelenweh, BWV 487. v. H. hat die Urlinie verfertigt, leider falsch. Eine Generalbaß-Aussetzung wäre ohne Kenntnis der Urlinie nicht ausführbar. Nach Schluß der Stunde greift H. noch auf Roth No 3Herman Roth, ed., 25 Geistliche Lieder: No. 3 Selig, wer an Jesum denkt, BWV 498. zurück, ich korrigire also auch das noch schnell, er bleibt bis ¾7h. Die Ueberdehnung der letzten Stunden erklärt sich – er verreist bis 15. XI.

15. XI Bericht über die Belgische Sammlung, wohin Stefan ZweigDiary Oct 23: “Stefan Zweig has visited the Photogram Archive and expressed his great enthusiasm about it.” den Weg gewiesen: nicht op. 106, sondern das Adagio aus dem Streichquartett op. 135 befindet sich dort, nebst dem Manuscript der Etude symphonique von Schumann,
Originalbriefen von Haydn usw. Ueber das Schnabl-Konzert;The recital by Artur Schnabel took place in the great hall of the Musikverein on November 4 at 12.30 p.m., program: Schubert, Sonata in C minor, D. 958; Mozart, Sonata in D major, K. 576; Beethoven, Diabelli Variations. ich spiele einzelne Stücke aus der Schubert Sonate Cm vor. Zeige den Unterschied von wirklichem u. üblichen Vortrag im einzelnen; aus dem letzten Satz die interessante Stelle: kompositionell den Weg I–III: diagram: graph Fasch gebe ich zurück. Nocturne Fisd, Studie der Ornamente; ich zeige einzelne Bilder u. Figuren zum 1. Satz der Eroica; er empfiehlt die Deutsche Notgemeinschaft.The Notgemeinschaft der deutschen Wissenschaft, an organization founded in 1920 to help distribute funds for the promotion of the sciences and humanities in Germany.

19. Bitte um Maschinenschrift zu op. 117, da meine Augen größter Schonung bedürfen.Op. 117: a study by Hoboken of Op. 117, Nos. 1–3, comparing the autograph with the Simrock and collected editions, which is preserved at OC 14/2 (28-page typescript) and OC 14/3 (earlier typewritten amended draft) — Diary Nov 19: “I succeed in persuading Hoboken to have his work typed, thus removing all traces of a quarrel.” op. 117II in Angriff genommen u. been-
-det. Gesd.-Etude, die Hände einzeln. Zur VII. Sinfonie einige noch ungelöste Stellen in Furtwänglers Vortrag.

22. Zeige in der Deutschen Tonkünstler Ztg. zwei Aufsätze, Schönberg u. Schmid, über mich;Diary Nov 24: “9:15 to 11, letter to Floriz[= OJ 6/7, [44]], [...] I mention facts concerning my successes [...]; the Deutsche Tonkünstler-Zeitung of November 11 which includes an essay by Schmid. Linked with Schmid's essay, I offer examples that would serve as a response to Schoenberg, in music illustrations and text: Bach Prelude in C minor from the Well-Tempered Clavier and the so-called "Dissonant" introduction to Mozart's Quartet in C major.” — The Deutsche Tonkünstler-Zeitung of November 5, 1929 (vol. 27, issue 21) contains both Schoenberg's Zur Frage des modernen Kompositionsunterrichtes and an essay by Waldemar Schmid. From the way Schenker punctuates this sentence, one would infer that both refer to him; but only Schmid mentions him by name. über Kontrapunkt überhaupt; zeige das neueste Lehrbuch von KrehlIt is not clear to which book Schenker is referring. Krehl died in 1924, and his counterpoint book, subtitled The Theory of Independent Voice Leading, was first published in 1908. u. die so einführende Nähe zum Freien Satz, wie doch auch schon bei Albrechtsberger dieser Irrtum sich findet. Spielt die Etude Gesd.

26. Korrigire Roth No 4Herman Roth, ed., 25 Geistliche Lieder (aus dem Schemellischen Gesangbuch) für eine Singstimme und basso continuo (Leipzig: C. F. Peters, [n.d.]), a copy of which, with annotations in Schenker's hand, is preserved at OJ 25/1: No. 4 Mein Jesu! was für Seelenweh, BWV 487.; zu Casals Konzert:The concert took place in the large hall of the Konzerthaus on Saturday November 30, with Pablo Casals, cello, and Otto Schulhof, piano; the program included Beethoven’s Sonata Op. 102, No. 2, and Bach’s unaccompanied Cello Suite in E major. Beethoven op. 102II; zeige im 1. Satz den 2. Ged. u. die Fuge ganz. Roth No 5: ibid., No. 5 Brich entzwei, mein armes Herze, BWV 444. korrigire die Linie; Schubert „Der Schiffer“ aus Bd. V.

29. Uebergibt mir op. 117III. Spielt nicht mehr! Chopin u. die Literatur, die ich auflege, will plötzlich Vierhändigkeiten, nicht aber etwa Brahms, sondern
Bruckner; beginnend mit der Sinf. IV, 1. u. 2. Satz – bis ¾7h.

tei:div.tei:ab: October 8: Concerning the Yearbook – or will it be a periodical? Hoboken would like the volumes to appear without time constraint. I ask myself when it will begin. Op. 117, No. 1: he notates my critique in his score.

October 11: On the execution of a turn figure – the Pro Arte Quartet is in error. Chopin etudes in C minor, A minor, and E minor revisited. Critique of the revision-study continued, No. 1 completed. I instruct him to work through my corrections anew.

October 15: Etude in E minor: I explain the dynamic markings on their intrinsic basis; technique,
performance, fingering. He gives me the corrected presentation of Op. 117, No. 1.
October 18: Etude in E minor played. I go through my corrections with him. Bach-Schemelli-Roth No. 1, neu.

October 22: I show him Oppel’s cantata and several mistakes in it. I ask for the manuscript from the Archive, if possible. Returning to Weisse, I show him a letter from Weisse sent to Galtür, in which he has absolutely expressed no decline in his estimation of me. Roth No. 2, new. He brings Musikalisches Mancherlei, which includes a sonata by C. P. E. Bach. He invites himself to my radio loudspeaker for Friday at 4:15 (!) to hear Pessel, we invite him for tea.

October 25: He arrives at 4 o’clock; then I offer my comments on Fasch’s sonata and C. P. Bach’s in G minor, played by Miss Pessel, with regard to voice-leading line and performance. Roth No. 3, line etc., in addition the edition by Breitkopf & Härtel. In the Etude in D major,
the hands worked through separately; he stays until 6:45!

October 29: On Furtwängler’s interpretation of Bruckner and Handel; on Walters performance of the “Haffner” Symphony: the Andante and Minuet from it played four-hands. Etude in G major, fingering and performance. Roth No. 4; Hoboken has completed the Urlinie, unfortunately incorrectly. A thoroughbass realization would not be possible without knowledge of the Urlinie. At the end of the lesson, Hoboken returns to Roth No. 3; I correct it, and thus also quickly; he stays until 6:45. The overexpansion of the last lessons is explained – he will be travelling until November 15.

November 15: Report on the Belgian collection, to which Stefan Zweig has pointed the way: it is not Op. 106 but the Adagio from the String Quartet Op. 135 that is found there, along with the autograph of the Études symphoniques by Schumann,
original letters by Haydn, and so on. Concerning Schnabel’s concert: I play to him individual pieces from Schubert’s Sonata in C minor. I show him the differences between true and commonplace performance in individual instances; from the last movement, the interesting passage in which the path from I to III is composed: diagram: graph. I return the sonata by Fasch. Nocturne in F major, study of the ornaments; I show him individual graphs and figures for the first movement of the Eroica; he recommends the German Emergency Association.

November 19: I ask him to type the study of Op. 117, as my eyes are in the direst need of being spared. Op. 117, No. 2 taken up and completed.
The Etude in G major, hands separately. Concerning the Seventh Symphony, a few still unresolved passages in Furtwängler’s performance.

November 22: I show him two essays in the Deutsche Tonkünstler-Zeitung, by Schoenberg u. Schmid, about me; about counterpoint in general. I show him Krehl’s latest textbook and its so seductive proximity to Free Composition, as this mistake is found already in Albrechtsberger. He plays the Etude in G major.

November 26: I correct Roth No. 4. On Casals’s concert: Beethoven Op. 102, No. 2; I show him the second theme in the first movement, and the entire fugue. Roth No. 5: I correct the voice-leading line; Schubert’s “Der Schiffer” from volume 5 of the Peters edition.

November 29: He gives me Op. 117, No. 3; he no longer plays! Chopin and the literature that I give him. Suddenly he wants to do four-hand stuff, but not something like Brahms but rather
Bruckner, beginning with the Fourth Symphony, first and second movements – stays until 6:45.
